do_not_assume: SaaS transfers ownership of Rock configuration.
A lower-cost provider supplies equivalent Rock expertise or service quality.
A proposed platform is the only way to solve the underlying problem.
goal: A documented hosting choice with explicit ownership, workload, security, and verification conditions.
steps: Restate the underlying organizational problem.
Produce distinct options that include at least SaaS hosting and self-managed hosting; include Azure only when it fits the requirements.
Inventory staff capacity, peak workload, public-site use, payment processing, integrations, plugins, customizations, availability goals, and budget constraints.
For each option, assign ownership for infrastructure, database, patches, certificates, domains, backups, monitoring, incidents, Rock configuration, users, and workflows.
Reject any single-server payment-processing topology.
Compare the options and record the unresolved live checks.
Stop when the selected model has a named owner for every operational responsibility.
title: Recipe: Select a hosting model

do_not_assume: Prices or nonprofit credits in an older excerpt remain current.
More memory alone resolves a CPU or database bottleneck.
goal: A provisional Azure tier supported by workload evidence and marked for validation.
steps: Record peak weekend attendance.
Select the corresponding starting tier from the current Rock Azure sizing table.
Move one tier larger if Rock hosts the public website.
Adjust for database size, feature intensity, analytics, reports, check-in, scheduled jobs, integrations, plugins, and growth.
Use the documented Windows VM plus Azure SQL pattern as the baseline.
Retrieve current Azure SKU availability and pricing before budgeting.
Define the telemetry and representative journeys that will validate the tier.
Stop when the baseline, assumptions, and post-provision validation plan are recorded.
title: Recipe: Build an Azure capacity baseline

do_not_assume: Do not treat generated guidance as live-instance proof.
goal: A provider-ready migration plan with a reserved test window and clear responsibility boundary.
steps: Choose the hosting partner and plan.
Inventory the current Rock version, database, files, domains, certificates, integrations, SMTP, plugins, custom code, jobs, and external dependencies.
Schedule the provider kickoff.
Define the migration sequence and rollback decision points.
Reserve a test period before public launch.
Confirm plan-specific responsibility for updates, backups, restores, certificates, domains, monitoring, incidents, and custom work.
Run representative administrative and public journeys in the migrated environment.
Stop before public launch if ownership, migration scope, or test results remain unresolved.
title: Recipe: Prepare a SaaS migration

do_not_assume: Verify the resulting resources and connections directly; do not rely on portal-screen similarity.
goal: A resource group containing the intended Rock web VM and Azure SQL resources.
steps: Create or select the Rock production resource group.
Provision the Windows web VM in that group.
Configure IIS on the web VM.
Provision the Azure SQL server and database in the same resource group.
Create Rock’s Azure SQL login and `master` user.
Grant `dbmanager` and `loginmanager`.
Run the Rock installation so the application database is created.
Create the Rock user in the application database and add it to `db_owner`.
Test the restricted Rock login.
Verify the resulting resources and connections directly; do not rely on portal-screen similarity.
title: Recipe: Provision the documented Azure layout

do_not_assume: Do not treat generated guidance as live-instance proof.
goal: A Windows/IIS host ready for the documented Rock 19 installer.
steps: Confirm the current Rock technical requirements and SQL Server requirement.
Install IIS, the applicable ASP.NET 4.x role service, WebSocket Protocol, Application Initialization, and .NET Framework 3.5 Features.
Configure the application pool for .NET Framework v4.0, automatic startup, `LocalSystem`, and zero idle timeout.
Configure a specific low-traffic recycling time.
Enable website preload.
Enable dynamic-content compression when the module is available.
Place only `Start.aspx` and `web.config` from the installer in the web root.
Open `/Start.aspx` locally.
Stop when the installer’s environmental checks pass.
Identify the database type: Azure SQL Database, SQL Server on an Azure VM, or local/self-hosted SQL Server.
Verify the server name, database name, Rock-specific login, and connection target without exposing the password.
For Azure SQL Database, verify the login and `master` user, the `dbmanager` and `loginmanager` roles, and the database user’s `db_owner` membership.
For a self-hosted two-server deployment, verify TCP 1433 is permitted from the Rock web server’s address.
Confirm that SQL Server is private rather than generally internet-exposed.
Test the Rock-specific SQL login independently.
Stop when the Rock web server can connect using the intended restricted identity and network path. Configure SQL Server
title: Recipe: Prepare an internal Rock 19 web server

do_not_assume: Do not treat generated guidance as live-instance proof.
goal: All expected Rock nodes are visible and coordinated without duplicate job runners.
steps: Obtain and record the Spark web-farm license.
Confirm that the gateway, database, web nodes, and Rock installations are running.
Configure session affinity at the gateway.
Move shared Rock File Types away from node-local storage or establish deliberate synchronization.
Configure one supported message-bus transport: Azure Service Bus or RabbitMQ.
Configure jobs to run on only one node.
Open `Admin Tools > System Settings > Web Farm`.
Activate the farm and enter the license.
Restart every web node.
Confirm every expected node appears on the Web Farm page.
Exercise cache-affecting changes, shared files, page routes, check-in sessions, and a scheduled job.
Stop when node membership, affinity, shared-file access, message-bus coordination, and single job execution are proven.
Confirm that the Spark web-farm license is active.
Confirm that exactly one supported message-bus transport is active.
Verify that the gateway, database, and expected web nodes are running.
Confirm that Rock is installed on each node.
Restart all nodes after web-farm activation or configuration changes.
Inspect the Web Farm page and web-farm log for startup, shutdown, status, or leadership events.
Confirm that every expected node appears.
Stop when node membership and message-bus communication are stable.
title: Recipe: Activate a Rock 19 web farm

do_not_assume: Do not treat generated guidance as live-instance proof.
goal: Eligible Rock 19 reporting or analytics traffic uses the intended read-only target.
steps: Confirm the read-only database or replica exists.
Determine whether the target workload is Data Views and Reports or the three supported analytics blocks.
Add `RockContextReadOnly` for Data Views and Reports, or `RockContextAnalytics` for Giving, Attendance, and Pledge Analytics.
Preserve the primary `RockContext`.
Test connectivity without exposing connection-string secrets.
Exercise each target workload.
For a Data View that requires writes, enable **Disable Use Of Read Only Context** on that Data View.
Observe which database receives the test traffic.
Stop when routing and write behavior match the intended design.
Confirm that `RockContextReadOnly` is present and points to the intended database.
Test basic connectivity and data availability.
Identify whether the Data View contains a plugin or filter that performs writes.
If writes are required, enable **Disable Use Of Read Only Context** for that specific Data View.
Retest the operation against the primary context.
Stop when the operation succeeds and its context selection is documented.
title: Recipe: Offload reports and analytics to a read-only database

do_not_assume: A slow page proves the server is undersized.
A clean trace rules out intermittent infrastructure issues.
Adding web nodes fixes database or custom-code constraints.
Stop when the slow component or infrastructure constraint is identified with repeatable evidence; do not prescribe a web farm solely from the symptom.
goal: A repeatable diagnosis identifies either a page component or a broader infrastructure constraint.
steps: Capture the affected URL, user context, time, and expected behavior.
Run the v19 Page Load Time diagnostic.
Identify the slowest page components.
Repeat the test to determine whether the result is stable.
Correlate it with IIS, CPU, database, storage, network, and provider telemetry.
Inspect snapshot isolation and supported read-only-context opportunities.
Record whether the cause is component-specific, database-related, capacity-related, intermittent, or unresolved.
Stop when the evidence supports a bounded next action.
Confirm the Rock version. In v19, capture the Page Load Time diagnostic trace for the affected page.
Identify whether one block or component dominates the trace.
Reproduce at a known time and record whether the issue is constant, intermittent, or load-dependent.
Inspect IIS application-pool startup, idle timeout, preload, recycling, and dynamic-compression settings.
Determine whether the page invokes Data Views, Reports, analytics, plugins, APIs, or long-running database operations.
Inspect whether snapshot isolation is enabled and whether supported read workloads are eligible for `RockContextReadOnly` or `RockContextAnalytics`. Install Rock
Compare the symptom with CPU, database, network, and provider telemetry.
Stop when the slow component or infrastructure constraint is identified with repeatable evidence; do not prescribe a web farm solely from the symptom.
title: Recipe: Diagnose a slow Rock 19 page

do_not_assume: Do not treat generated guidance as live-instance proof.
goal: A go/no-go record separates verified readiness from unresolved conditions.
steps: Confirm the exact Rock, Windows, IIS, and SQL versions against current requirements.
Confirm topology and PCI-required web/database separation.
Inspect SQL network exposure and allowed TCP 1433 sources.
Validate HTTPS for internal and external Rock sites.
Confirm backup ownership, retention, and a tested restore path.
Confirm patch ownership and supported Rock branch.
Verify SMTP through a controlled delivery test.
Confirm file-storage behavior, especially across multiple nodes.
Confirm the single job-running node for Rock 19 farms.
Exercise representative public, administrative, check-in, reporting, and integration journeys.
Record unresolved gaps and assign owners.
Stop before launch if a security, payment-processing, recovery, certificate, or critical-path dependency remains unverified.
title: Recipe: Perform a pre-launch infrastructure review
